
## Methods

<!-- Datasets
 -->

The general scheme of analysis is presented in @fig-pipeline.

![Schematic analysis pipeline.](figures/chapter2/pipeline.png){#fig-pipeline height="60%" column="page"}

### Intracranial data

The intracranial EEG data were obtained from the MNI Open iEEG Atlas [@frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial], a normative resource compiled from 106 patients with refractory epilepsy  recorded at three centres. Only channels implanted in brain regions that were determined to be non-epileptogenic throughout the monitoring period were retained, yielding 1772 channels (13 channels were removed from intitial release as were later judged erroneus on visual inspection) distributed across 38 cortical regions defined by the MICCAI atlas. @fig-frauscher-atlas provides a spatial overview of channel coverage in the atlas, distinguishing depth/stereo-EEG contacts from cortical grid and strip contacts across both hemispheres.

These 38 regions were derived from the consolidation of 20 smaller MICCAI labels into 8 functional groups to ensure sufficient channel density (min. 5 per region), while 16 labels were omitted due to lack of coverage. For each channel, 60 seconds of resting wakefulness data with eyes closed were available.
Atlas authors resampled signals to 200 Hz and  applied low-pass antialiasing filter at 80 Hz and power-line interference was reduced with an adaptive filter. Power spectral density (PSD) was estimated using Welch's method with 2-second Hamming windows and 50% overlap, resulting in a frequency resolution of 0.5 Hz.  Full preprocessing details are given in @frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial.


### Source-reconstructed HD-EEG

Five minutes  of eyes-open resting state EEG data were collected in 19 healthy young adult volunteers (age $28\pm 6$ years, 14 females) with Ethics Committee of ETH Zurich approval. EEG signals were recorded at 1000Hz sampling rate using a 256channel HydroCel Geodesic Sensor Net by Electrical Geodesics (Eugene, Oregon, USA). HD-EEG data were recorded with eyes open condition.
The full details of collecting and preprocessing this dataset dataset were described in @samogin2019SharedConnectionspecificIntrinsic and  @samogin2020FrequencydependentFunctionalConnectivity.  The poor  chanels were  identified (0-13 pers subject) and interpolated, data was band-pass filtered within 1-80Hz range and biological artifact were removed using fixed-point ICA (FastICA) algorithm. The realistic head model was provided as input to the exact low-resolution brain electromagnetic tomography (eLORETA) algorithm [@pascual-marqui2011AssessingInteractionsBrain], together with the  preprocessed EEG signals, to estimate brain activity in the source space at high-temporal resolution.

 The  following steps and timeseries extraction were chosen to  matche the iEEG atlas: source activity was extracted from reconstructed sources  using average coordinates from the  electrodes within 76 MICCAI-defined ROIs in MNI space,  resulting in 1444 virtual sensors, with the grouped regional reference coordinates illustrated in Figure @fig-frauscher-atlas, panel B.

For every virtual sensor 60s activity was extracted according to the parameters defined in Frauscher's paper (sampling frequency 200Hz). Spectral densities were computed using identical Welch parameters (2s windows, 50% overlap, 0.5 Hz resolution). 

All spectral data were normalized to unit total power to ensure that the comparison focused on the distribution of frequency peaks (e.g., the occipital alpha or hippocampal delta) rather than absolute amplitude differences between scalp and intracranial sensors.

## Oscillatory descriptors

#### K-means clusterisation

For direct comparison with the original atlas, we followed the peak-detection procedure of @frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial.
The normalised power spectra were classified into k groups using k-means with 160 features (0.5 Hz bins from 0.5 to 80 Hz), Euclidean distance, and 100 repetitions. The classification was repeated with increasing k until a group without peaks was identified, defined as the group whose mean normalised spectrum was lower than the maximum among the other groups. The 50% of channels
closest to the group mean were retained as the no-peak set.

To test for the presence of region-specific peaks against this no-peak reference set, the spectrum was divided into frequency intervals. The 160 frequency bins were grouped into 22 frequency intervals based on the condition that each bin contains at least 4% of total mean power, yielding
boundaries at 0.5, 0.75, 1.25, 1.75, 2.25, 3.25, 3.75, 4.25, 5.25, 6.25, 6.75, 7.75, 8.25, 9.25, 10.25, 11.75, 13.25, 15.25, 17.25, 20.25, 24.25, 31.75, and 80 Hz. 

The presence of a peak in a given frequency interval for a particular brain region was determined by comparing the distribution of spectral densities of all channels in that region against the no-peak set, using a one-sided two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test at the 5% significance level with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons across 42 regions (38 cortical regions plus 4 lobes) and 22 frequency intervals (hemispheres grouped together).

The Kolmogorov-Smirnov screen identifies where a region differs from the no-peak set but not how many of its channels drive that difference. To quantify how widespread the effect was within the region each channel's relative power in that interval was compared against the no-peak distribution with a one-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum (Mann-Whitney U) test at the 5% level, uncorrected. We report the proportion of the region's channels that exceeded the no-peak set. This second stage mirrors the two-step logic of @frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial.

For the HD-EEG data, the same procedure was applied with the
iEEG-derived frequency intervals retained for comparability, even though the 4% power condition was not met for the source-reconstructed spectra.
<!-- Implications of this deviation are reported as a finding (Section 3.1.1). -->


### Cross-modal correspondence on uncorrected spectra

Cross-modal agreement between the iEEG atlas and the source-reconstructed HD-EEG was quantified using the band-overlap metric of @afnan2024ValidationMEGSource, applied directly to the unit-power-normalised PSDs. Channels were pooled across hemispheres by grouping on the hemisphere-agnostic MICCAI region name, collapsing left and right ROIs into the 38 bilateral regions of the atlas. Within each region $r$, the iEEG atlas was taken as the reference modality and the HD-EEG source data as the estimated modality. Let $\widetilde{L}_r(f)$ denote the median of the log-PSD across the channels of region $r$ at frequency bin $f$, and $\text{SD}^{\,\text{HD}}_r(f)$ the corresponding standard deviation in HD-EEG. The bin-wise overlap is

$$
\text{overlap}_r(f) =
\begin{cases}
    1 - \dfrac{\bigl\lvert \widetilde{L}^{\,\text{iEEG}}_r(f) - \widetilde{L}^{\,\text{HD}}_r(f) \bigr\rvert}
              {\text{SD}^{\,\text{HD}}_r(f)},
        & \bigl\lvert \widetilde{L}^{\,\text{iEEG}}_r(f) - \widetilde{L}^{\,\text{HD}}_r(f) \bigr\rvert
          \le \text{SD}^{\,\text{HD}}_r(f) \\[2mm]
    0,  & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
$$


The metric equals 1 when the iEEG median lands exactly on the HD-EEG median and decreases linearly to 0 once the two medians differ by one HD-EEG standard deviation. The bin-wise overlap was averaged across the frequency bins of each canonical band ($\delta$ 0.5-4, $\theta$ 4-8, $\alpha$ 8-13, $\beta$ 13-30, $\gamma$ 30-80 Hz), yielding one value per region per band. Both the unaveraged bin-level overlap and the band-averaged summary are reported.


## Spectral parametrisation

#### specparam settings

PSDs were parameterised using specparam (formerly FOOOF; @donoghue2020ParameterizingNeuralPower) with the following shared settings:

- Fitting frequency range: 1-80 Hz (primary); 1-45 Hz (range comparison
  in Section )
- Peak width limits: 1.0-8.0 Hz
- Maximum number of peaks: 8
- Minimum peak height: 0.1 (log power)
- Peak threshold: 3.0 standard deviations of the residual

Model fits were evaluated using R² and mean absolute error; fits with R²
below 0.90 were flagged for inspection and the sensitivity of regional
results to their inclusion or exclusion was assessed (Section x.x).


###  Aperiodic parametrisation and model selection

Two aperiodic models are used. In **fixed** mode the aperiodic component
is modelled in log-power space as

$$L_{\mathrm{ap}}(f) = b - \chi \cdot \log_{10}(f)$$

with offset b and exponent χ. In **knee** mode,

$$L_{\mathrm{ap}}(f) = b - \log_{10}(k + f^{\chi})$$

with an additional knee parameter k.

The aperiodic mode for each modality was chosen based on  Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC)  choosing  knee or fixed mode similarly like in @ameen2025TemporallyResolvedAnalyses. 

The iEEG atlas exhibits a clear knee in log-log space, as
originally reported by @frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial and consistent with reports that knees are common in intracranial recordings [@ameen2025TemporallyResolvedAnalyses; @bush2024AperiodicComponentsLocal];
<!-- ; the knee model is therefore used for iEEG. HD-EEG
source-reconstructed spectra are typically near-linear in log-log space
across the fitted range, where the fixed model is the standard choice
(Donoghue et al. 2020); the fixed model is therefore used for HD-EEG.
BIC values for both modes are reported per modality (Section 3.2.1) as

####  Per-band peak prevalence from specparam

For each channel, parameterised peaks from specparam (Section 2.4) were
assigned to canonical bands δ (0.5-4 Hz), θ (4-8 Hz), α (8-13 Hz), β
(13-30 Hz), and γ (30-80 Hz) according to their centre frequency. Peak
prevalence in a region was defined as the proportion of channels in that
region exhibiting at least one peak in a given band.


###  Aperiodic subtraction

The fitted aperiodic component was reconstructed on the fitted frequency
grid and subtracted from the empirical PSD in linear power space, yielding
the residual

$$\mathrm{PSD}_{\mathrm{osc}}(f) = \mathrm{PSD}(f) - \mathrm{PSD}_{\mathrm{ap}}(f)$$

This is the primary residual used throughout. A log-ratio alternative,
L_osc(f) = log10(PSD(f) / PSD_ap(f)), corresponding to the specparam
convention, is reported as a sensitivity comparison.

####  IRASA

As a complementary decomposition, aperiodic exponents in HD-EEG were also
estimated using Irregular Resampling Auto-Spectral Analysis (IRASA; Wen
and Liu 2016). IRASA computes the power spectrum at multiple resampling
factors (h = 1.05 to 2.0 in steps of 0.05); for each factor, the
geometric mean of the up-sampled and down-sampled spectra is taken, and
the median across factors yields the fractal (aperiodic) component.
Because IRASA up-samples the signal by up to h_max = 2, the analysed band
is bounded by the Nyquist limit, h_max · f_hi < f_s / 2. With f_s = 200 Hz
this restricts the upper edge to below 50 Hz, so the IRASA decomposition
was run over 2-40 Hz. The fractal exponent was obtained by fitting a line
in log-log space to the IRASA aperiodic spectrum; the sign-reversed slope
is the IRASA exponent.



### Stability analyses

<!-- FIX #5: clarified which of the three stability comparisons feed the
Bayesian model and which are reported separately. Previous version listed
three comparisons in bold and then said "the range and modality comparisons
are pooled", but "modality" wasn't one of the listed comparisons — modality
enters the Bayesian model as a fixed-effect adjustment, not as a stability
comparison in its own right. -->
Three stability comparisons are performed on the aperiodic estimates.

**Knee vs fixed.** For each modality, the channel-level exponent estimated
under the knee model is compared with the channel-level exponent estimated
under the fixed model. Because the two exponents are not on the same
scale, the comparison is by Pearson and Spearman rank correlation across
channels.

**Fitting range.** For each modality, the fixed-mode exponent is computed
over 1-80 Hz and over 1-45 Hz. Per-channel agreement between the two
estimates is quantified.

**IRASA vs specparam at matched band.** For HD-EEG, IRASA exponents over
2-40 Hz are compared with specparam fixed-mode exponents refit over the
same 2-40 Hz band, by Pearson and Spearman correlation across channels.

Of these, the fitting-range comparison is pooled into a hierarchical
Bayesian regression with the exponent as the outcome, fitting range as
the predictor of interest, modality as a fixed-effect adjustment, and ROI
and subject as random effects, with a random slope of range over ROI to
localise where the choice of range materially shifts the estimate. The
knee-vs-fixed and IRASA-vs-specparam comparisons are reported separately
as rank correlations.
